en: Suffering oppression, from Talas
How can I forget my flight?
Do not scatter my thoughts, God.
You made them call another man's son
The child born from my belly.
Do not dig my pit, God;
God, do not boil my bitter fate any further.
Making them call me a fugitive woman,
O God, do not bring strange trials upon me.
Do not let a bird of prey eat the swan.
In this Bukhara here,
Do not let them call me a ruined woman.
Do not let a bird of prey eat the goose.
In this Bukhara here,
Do not let them call me a fugitive woman.
I have no strength to give me support.
If I race Taytoru to divine my fate,
To urge him on without grieving me,
My supportive Kyrgyz people are not here.
If I struggle, no one takes account of me.
If I make this my divination,
To urge him on without shame,
My Kyrgyz kin are not here.
I have no support to lean on.
To face the task with honor held firm,
To urge him on steadfastly,
The renowned Kyrgyz are not here.
Seen today, gone tomorrow—
Distracting me like this,
You deceive me, shitty world!
Who will rejoice and show affection
To a widow like me?
If I do not die today, let me divine my fate
With my swift horse Taytoru.
If my Bay comes in front,
Let me share out the highest prize.
To my lord who went to the other world,
To his spirit I shall pray;
This Bay horse here,
Let me race to divine my fate.
If my Bay comes through,
Let me share out the highest prize.
If Taytoru does not come through,
Rather than be called a shameless woman,
Let me die before my appointed death.
If things become as they once were,
Jylgynduu, Keng-Kol, broad Talas—
If the one God grants me my river valley,
And settles me in my valley;
If what was severed is joined,
If what was scattered is gathered,
If my fly-like little soul rejoices,
If for this sorrowing head
There is a night like the Night of Power;
If the blessed Kyrgyz
God lets me see again,
If a day comes to return and see them,
With my weeping stilled,
My eyes fully refreshed;
If God brings me to Talas,
If a day comes for me to die there;
The sovereign Kyrgyz, my dear people,
If a day comes to see them,
My horse Taytoru, come through!
If all I grasp is burning coals,
If I have not a tiny share of blessing,
My horse Taytoru, fall behind."
Unable to stand for thinking and weeping,
Your sister-in-law beat herself in anguish.
To Manas, gone to the other world,
To his spirit she pleaded.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Resolved to draw the line,
Resolved to make a spectacle.
Racing her horse while in mourning,
She resolved to stir up trouble in Bukhara.
Until the appointed day arrived,
She fed him barnyard millet from the rice,
And sweated him every day.
Hanging up a bag of barley feed,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Of the courser Taytoru
She drew the sweat each month.
As dusk fell and the sun set,
Before the people lay down in silence,
She hurriedly recited her prayers.
Your grieving sister-in-law was anxious.
Unseen by a single soul,
She saddled Taytoru,
To send him over the open steppe,
From the noble, swift courser
To draw the bitter sweat,
And bring him into condition.
After that, the courser
She would race before the peoples of eight khans.
Of the courser Taytoru,
To test the length of his stride,
To send him over the open steppe,
To draw the foul sweat from his bones,
The gated city of Bukhara,
To its rear side,
To Sary-Talaa of broad Bukhara,
To the edge of great Ak-Chiy,
Your formidable mother Kanykey
Struck with her whip to left and right,
Spurring on either side.
Great Ak-Chiy of broad Bukhara,
With no hill even the size of a knucklebone,
With no hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
On that blade-flat yellow steppe,
Racing the flying birds,
With the accursed courser's
Mouth she struggled.
The great rein, braided in the okoro pattern,
In your dignified, fierce sister-in-law's
Palm pulled taut.
She sent him over the settled sand,
Making him gallop in surging bounds,
And drew his bitter sweat.
Round the jutting spur of the mountain
Your sister-in-law circled ten times.
Bounding and gathering himself,
The courser beneath her
Lowered his head toward the ground.
His feet pounded on the earth,
The black steel bit
Clattering in his throat.
Racing the flying birds,
With the truly spirit-like courser's
Mouth she struggled.
When he ran downhill,
His forelegs planted like a roe deer's.
When he turned uphill,
His mane and tail streamed out.
Unfortunate, with a hero's frame—
Could a woman be like this?
Such a fierce one as this,
People, can calling her a woman bring you good?
Taytoru, brought into racing condition,
Rumbled as though about to fly.
The sweat coming from his bones
Dripped down past his hooves.
His foul sweat poured away;
All his ribs
Stood apart like whip handles.
When she turned and came back,
Your dignified, fierce sister-in-law's,
Kanykey's white palace
Had an iron door of solid tin.
However much a fugitive she was,
Your sister-in-law kept her dignity.
She had much stateliness.
To the plane tree before the house,
The precious woman Kanykey
The courser Taytoru's
Saddle she removed, leaving him bare,
And brought the courser over.
Tethering him high, binding his lower leg,
She tied him up high,
And left him standing through the night.
When dawn broke bright,
When light touched the earth,
The stars trembled in the sky,
One by one toward the qibla.
Stars scattered from overhead,
And dawn opened bright.
The lord's wife Kanykey
Walked to the plane tree,
And the courser Taytoru
She untied from the plane tree.
She put him to good grazing.
Leading him a little,
She kept at it without tiring,
Filling his stomach with grass.
Ten fescues, eighty grasses,
Letting him crop them in swathes;
With the surging spring water
She quenched his thirst.
Grieving and calling on God,
She put his bit back in.
It was the time of midmorning.
To the copper post in the palace
She tied him up high.
The rich, patterned horsecloth
Your sister-in-law gently took off.
The courser Taytoru
She scraped with a scraper,
And struck him with a ramrod.
She drew his covering back,
And wiped his sweat clean.
Until death, her words were frank;
While alive, your sister-in-law was clear-sighted.
After she had wiped his sweat,
When she looked at Taytoru,
Who raced the flying birds,
The belly flesh from which fat is taken
On Taytoru had become
Pressed against his lower ribs.
His eyes flashed like the Morning Star.
Without bristling, his hairs lay separate.
He looked to either side,
Licking his lips and muzzle.
The black steel bit
He knocked against his throat.
His tail, like strands of silk,
He lashed against his thighs.
So Taytoru had become.
Grinding and gnawing his teeth,
Tearing up the ground he trod,
So Taytoru had become.
"This dear courser of mine,
Unless my ill fortune prevents it,
Will lower his head to the ground.
Without letting them call me a wandering woman,
Today, of Bukhara
He will take the highest prize.
But if it does not happen, what shall I do?
Today I, this fierce woman,
Will braid the hair down my back.
Without letting them call me a shameless woman,
If Taytoru falls behind,
I shall die before my appointed death.
My forehead bone was sloping;
After the sovereign passed away,
I, this fierce woman, was left like this,
With few days left to live.
An iron net was drawn beneath me.
If Taytoru falls behind,
What will become of our ill fortune?"
Her thoughts are torn with sorrow.
At that moment, the fierce woman's
Tears pour from her eyes.
"I have no forest to flee into,
No support to lean on,
No people to rely upon."
So Taytoru stood.
"Would that ill-fated one find good fortune,
That one who had been wandering in flight—
Saying, 'It is a fugitive's horse,'
Would he block my horse's path?
Making me feel my solitude,
Tormenting my soul like this,
The courser Taytoru,
If he should come in front,
Would they seize him on the road?
Bringing him onto the road,
Would they trample him underfoot?
If some wretch comes to no good,
If he blocks my horse's path,
If he wishes it, let me seize him,
Every khan who interferes.
Would some wretch find good fortune,
Saying, 'It is a woman's horse,'
And suddenly block his path?
Who would show affection
To a widow like me?
